power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007) for a mixed-model design with 2 within-subject x 2 between-subject conditions. Assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), α = .05, desired power of .90, and a correlation of .50 between repeated measures, the required sample size to detect a within-subject main effect (Hypothesis 1a) was 68, and detecting a within x between-subject interaction (Hypothesis 1b) also required 68 participants. Detecting additional moderation or mediation effects (Hypothesis 2) was estimated to require 130 participants. Because data collection could not be extended beyond June 2024, the final sample consisted of 114 participants, providing sufficient power to test Hypotheses 1a and 1b, and approximately .80 power for Hypothesis 2. We paid participants €10.00, or 2 ECTS, for their full participation.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Coping with the Threat of Social Change: Study 3
table.research_questions:
Hypotheses:
(1) Social change will elicit a stronger threat response than the status quo.

(2) Minoritized group members (i.e., LGBTQ+ people) will experience lower threat appraisal than dominant group members (i.e., cishet people).

(3) Minoritized group members (i.e., LGBTQ+ people) will experience higher challenge appraisal than dominant group members (i.e., cishet people) in response to social change.

(4) Perceived demands, and uncertainty of social change will positively meditate the relationship between social change and threat appraisal. Perceived resources to deal with social change will negatively meditate the relationship between social change and threat appraisal.

(5) Higher threat appraisal will lead to more rigid (than open), more instrumental (than symbolic), more negative (than positive), more self-related and ingroup-related (than system-related) arguments.

Exploratory questions:
(1) Higher threat appraisal will lead to preference for individual focus policies (vs. system focus policies).

(2) Higher threat appraisal will lead lower action intentions in support for LGBTQ+ rights.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: 2 (scenario: status quo vs. social change) within-subject x 2 (group membership: cishet vs. LGBTQ+) (quasi) between-subject design.
table.randomization: Participants will not be randomly assigned to one of the two between-subject conditions (i.e., group membership: cishet vs. LGBTQ+), as we will consider people's actual belonging to one of these group. This condition is therefore quasi-experimental.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited at the Utrecht University campus and in the city of Utrecht more broadly, using a combination of online recruitment (SONA System, social media) and offline recruitment (poster, flyers, approaching people in person). Participants need to be at least 18 years old to take part in the study. They will be paid €10 or 2 PPU (credits) for their participation in the whole study.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 130. Considering that some data will be lost due to issues with the physiological measurements (i.e., ECG and blood pressure) we will reach a sample of 140 participants.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We used the software program G*Power to conduct a power analysis. Our goal is to obtain .90 power to detect a somewhat medium effect size of .20 at the standard .05 alpha error probability, and assuming a .50 correlation among repeated measures. Given the mixed design method of our study, we considered results to three power analyses:

ANOVA: Repeated measures, within factors: recommends N = 68 (hypothesis 1).
ANOVA: Repeated measures, within-between interaction: recommends N = 68 (hypothesis 2, and 3).
Linear multiple regression: Fixed model, R^2 deviation from zero: recommends N = 130  (hypothesis 4, and 5).
table.stopping_rule: Inspection of the quality of the physiological data is possible during the experimental session is ongoing. If suspicion arise that the data of a certain number of participants will be lost due to poor physiological data quality, we will collect more data than the 135 initially considered in order to compensate for such loss.
table.manipulated_variables:
We manipulated the scenario participants are exposed to, using written texts. 

Each participant is first presented with a text describing the status quo regarding transgender and non-binary people's rights in the Netherlands. Afterwards, participants read about immanent social changes regarding transgender and non-binary people's rights in the Netherlands.

Following current literature on social change, the texts in particular manipulate three aspects:
(1) Establishment vs. Change
(2) Stability vs. Instability
(3) Certainty vs. Uncertainty
table.measured_variables:
Main independent variables (manipulated/naturally occurring): 
- scenario (status quo, social change)
- group membership (dominant/cishet, marginalized/LGBTQ+)

Manipulation check: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree.
- novelty of the topic
- credibility of the topic
- severity of change
- change derived instability
- change derived uncertainty

Main dependent variables: 
- physiological markers of threat and challenge appraisal (HR, PEP, CO, TPR), using a combination of impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG) and continuous blood pressure (BP). 
- 2-minute speech on participant's opinion about the text they read, looking at rigidity (change between speech 1 and 2), arguments type (instrumental, symbolic), arguments focus (system, ingroup, self, others), opinion valence (scale from 1 to 9).

Biopsychosocial model variables: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree. Each item is measured at four levels: personal, ingroup, outgroup system.
- self reported threat vs. challenge of [status quo/social change] 9-item scale (instrumental, morality, identity sub-scales)
- self reported engagement with [status quo/social change]
- self reported demands of [status quo/social change] 3-item scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)
- self reported resources of [status quo/social change] 3-item scale (resources, skills and knowledge, support)

- self reported threat of delivering the speech
- self reported challenge of delivering the speech
- self reported engagement with delivering the speech
- self reported demands of delivering the speech 3 item-scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)
- self reported resources of delivering the speech 3-item scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)

Covariates: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree
- attitudes transgender and non-binary people 20-item scale
- identification with one's ingroup (straight/LGBTQ+) 14-item scale
- solidarity with the outgroup (cishet/LGBTQ+) 3-item scale
- identification with minority's cause 6-item scale

Demographics:
- political orientation (1 = right, 9 = left)
- age
- higher degree obtained
- faculty of study
- family income
- personal income
- occupation
- subjective social status (SSS)
- sex
- gender
- sexual orientation
- nationality
- ethnicity
- mental and/or physical disability

Exploratory variables:
- policy preference
- action intention (individual and collective) 65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 coping with social change_study 3_measured variables.docx https://osf.io/project/pvqka/files/osfstorage/65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 https://osf.io/download/65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 b4e06bf33a37888b4ab82e25c813c853d321a1c338df80ddc9bd1033d77bd3dd
table.indices:
Physiological markers of threat and challenge appraisal (HR, PEP, CO, TPR), using a combination of impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG) and continuous blood pressure (BP). These will summarized in an Engagement index (ENGI) and a Threat and Challenge index (TCI)

Manipulation check: severity, stability and uncertainty are combined in degree of social change.

Biopsychosocial model variables: average score combining levels, and scale items if applicable.

Covariates: average scores of the various scales.
table.statistical_tests:
Hypotheses testing:
(1) To test our hypotheses 1, 2, and 3 we will use step-wise multilevel modeling (lmer in R Studio). The model will include the interaction effect between scenario x group membership as main predictors, followed by main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).

(2) To test our hypotheses 4 we will use Hayes Mediation Models (PROCESS Macro in SPSS). The model will include perceived degree of social change as independent variable, and TCI as dependent variable. the mediators tested will be uncertainty, demands and resources of social change.

(3) To test our hypotheses 5 we will use step-wise multilevel modeling (lmer in R Studio). The model will include TCI as main predictor, followed by main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).
table.inference_criteria: We will use a combination of p<.05 criteria and 95% confidence intervals for determining whether our hypotheses were correct.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data may be excluded based on the quality of the physiological data.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Exploratory analyses:
(1) Mediation model as in (2), but the main dependent variable is self-reported TCI.

(2) Mediation model as in (2), but the mediators are the speech related demands and resources.

(3) To explore question 1, and 2 we will run multiple regression analyses. The models will include TCI (physiological and self-reported) and main predictors, and policy preference (model 1)/action intentions (model 2) as dependent variables, main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).

Additional analyses:
(1) EFA to analyze the structure of the scale of Attitudes toward Transgender and non-binary people.

(2) CFA to analyze the reliability of the scales of attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment.

(3) Descriptive analyses per variable, and correlation matrix of main variables to explore correlations.

ANOVA: Repeated measures, within-between interaction: recommends N = 68 (hypothesis 2, and 3).
Linear multiple regression: Fixed model, R^2 deviation from zero: recommends N = 130  (hypothesis 4, and 5).
table.stopping_rule: Inspection of the quality of the physiological data is possible during the experimental session is ongoing. If suspicion arise that the data of a certain number of participants will be lost due to poor physiological data quality, we will collect more data than the 135 initially considered in order to compensate for such loss.
table.manipulated_variables:
We manipulated the scenario participants are exposed to, using written texts. 

Each participant is first presented with a text describing the status quo regarding transgender and non-binary people's rights in the Netherlands. Afterwards, participants read about immanent social changes regarding transgender and non-binary people's rights in the Netherlands.

Following current literature on social change, the texts in particular manipulate three aspects:
(1) Establishment vs. Change
(2) Stability vs. Instability
(3) Certainty vs. Uncertainty
table.measured_variables:
Main independent variables (manipulated/naturally occurring): 
- scenario (status quo, social change)
- group membership (dominant/cishet, marginalized/LGBTQ+)

Manipulation check: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree.
- novelty of the topic
- credibility of the topic
- severity of change
- change derived instability
- change derived uncertainty

Main dependent variables: 
- physiological markers of threat and challenge appraisal (HR, PEP, CO, TPR), using a combination of impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG) and continuous blood pressure (BP). 
- 2-minute speech on participant's opinion about the text they read, looking at rigidity (change between speech 1 and 2), arguments type (instrumental, symbolic), arguments focus (system, ingroup, self, others), opinion valence (scale from 1 to 9).

Biopsychosocial model variables: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree. Each item is measured at four levels: personal, ingroup, outgroup system.
- self reported threat vs. challenge of [status quo/social change] 9-item scale (instrumental, morality, identity sub-scales)
- self reported engagement with [status quo/social change]
- self reported demands of [status quo/social change] 3-item scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)
- self reported resources of [status quo/social change] 3-item scale (resources, skills and knowledge, support)

- self reported threat of delivering the speech
- self reported challenge of delivering the speech
- self reported engagement with delivering the speech
- self reported demands of delivering the speech 3 item-scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)
- self reported resources of delivering the speech 3-item scale (demands, efforts, uncertainty)

Covariates: 9-point Likert scale self-reported, 1 = completely disagree, 9 = completely agree
- attitudes transgender and non-binary people 20-item scale
- identification with one's ingroup (straight/LGBTQ+) 14-item scale
- solidarity with the outgroup (cishet/LGBTQ+) 3-item scale
- identification with minority's cause 6-item scale

Demographics:
- political orientation (1 = right, 9 = left)
- age
- higher degree obtained
- faculty of study
- family income
- personal income
- occupation
- subjective social status (SSS)
- sex
- gender
- sexual orientation
- nationality
- ethnicity
- mental and/or physical disability

Exploratory variables:
- policy preference
- action intention (individual and collective) 65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 coping with social change_study 3_measured variables.docx https://osf.io/project/pvqka/files/osfstorage/65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 https://osf.io/download/65b7d41bb1f2b50ac8b0eb38 b4e06bf33a37888b4ab82e25c813c853d321a1c338df80ddc9bd1033d77bd3dd
table.indices:
Physiological markers of threat and challenge appraisal (HR, PEP, CO, TPR), using a combination of impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG) and continuous blood pressure (BP). These will summarized in an Engagement index (ENGI) and a Threat and Challenge index (TCI)

Manipulation check: severity, stability and uncertainty are combined in degree of social change.

Biopsychosocial model variables: average score combining levels, and scale items if applicable.

Covariates: average scores of the various scales.
table.statistical_tests:
Hypotheses testing:
(1) To test our hypotheses 1, 2, and 3 we will use step-wise multilevel modeling (lmer in R Studio). The model will include the interaction effect between scenario x group membership as main predictors, followed by main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).

(2) To test our hypotheses 4 we will use Hayes Mediation Models (PROCESS Macro in SPSS). The model will include perceived degree of social change as independent variable, and TCI as dependent variable. the mediators tested will be uncertainty, demands and resources of social change.

(3) To test our hypotheses 5 we will use step-wise multilevel modeling (lmer in R Studio). The model will include TCI as main predictor, followed by main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).
table.inference_criteria: We will use a combination of p<.05 criteria and 95% confidence intervals for determining whether our hypotheses were correct.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data may be excluded based on the quality of the physiological data.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Exploratory analyses:
(1) Mediation model as in (2), but the main dependent variable is self-reported TCI.

(2) Mediation model as in (2), but the mediators are the speech related demands and resources.

(3) To explore question 1, and 2 we will run multiple regression analyses. The models will include TCI (physiological and self-reported) and main predictors, and policy preference (model 1)/action intentions (model 2) as dependent variables, main covariates (attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment), and demographics variables (gender, political orientation, ethnicity, socio-economic status).

Additional analyses:
(1) EFA to analyze the structure of the scale of Attitudes toward Transgender and non-binary people.

(2) CFA to analyze the reliability of the scales of attitudes, identification, outgroup solidarity, minority cause investment.

(3) Descriptive analyses per variable, and correlation matrix of main variables to explore correlations.

In keeping with Hypothesis 1a, participants exhibited lower CO in the social change condition than in the status quo condition, β = -0.16, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.30, -0.03], p = .019.

The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was not significant, β = -0.11, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.06], p = .189, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, the effect of social change did not differ between cishet and LGBTQ+ participants.
Notably, trans participants exhibited significantly lower CO, β = -0.25, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.46, -0.05], p = .016.

table.formatted: Finally, the effect of minoritized status was moderated by GTS, β = -1.19, SE = 0.54, 95% CI [-2.27, -0.12], p = .030, such that LGBTQ+ participants higher in transphobia exhibited lower CO (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

Contrary to Hypothesis 1a, participants exhibited similar TPR across state of change conditions, β = 0.04, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.20], p = .662.

table.formatted: The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was significant, β = 0.21, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.41], p = .036, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited higher TPR in the social change condition compared to cishet participants (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

The interaction between minoritized status and being a woman was also significant, β = 0.31, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 0.61], p = .044, indicating higher TPR among LGBTQ+ participants identifying as women.

The interaction between minoritized status and OPS was marginally significant, β = 0.41, SE = 0.22, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.84], p = .063, suggesting that TPR may be higher among LGBTQ+ participants with greater solidarity with cishet individuals.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "\"Duurzaamheid betekent in staat zijn om voldoende middelen, zoals voedsel en kleding, te produceren om te leven, en tegelijkertijd de natuur voldoende tijd te geven om zichzelf te herstellen. Nederland heeft geprobeerd een zeker evenwicht te bereiken tussen productie en natuurherstel door het nemen van duurzaamheidsmaatregelen, zoals investeringen in windenergie. Windenergie is een pijler van het Nederlandse duurzaamheidsbeleid en dit zal nog lang vrijwel hetzelfde blijven. Wat betreft andere mogelijke duurzaamheidsvoorschriften is er minder voortgang geboekt.\"", 
"\"Gender en seksuele diversiteit (GSD), of simpelweg seksuele diversiteit, verwijst naar alle diversiteit van geslachtskenmerken, seksuele geaardheden en genderidentiteiten. Nederland heeft getracht een zekere tolerantie jegens GSD te bereiken door zogenaamde diversiteits- en inclusiemaatregelen, zoals de invoering van het homohuwelijk. Het homohuwelijk is een pijler van het Nederlandse GSD-beleid en dit zal nog lang vrijwel hetzelfde blijven. Wat betreft andere mogelijke GSD voorschriften is er minder voortgang geboekt.\"", 
"\"Het is zeer waarschijnlijk dat in de nabije toekomst verandering zal plaatsvinden wat betreft een andere aspect van duurzaamheidsmaatregelen in Nederland. Voedselverspilling zal binnenkort aanzienlijk worden teruggebracht met de introductie van verschillende beperkingen op hoeveel en wat voor soort voedsel er kan worden geproduceerd in en geïmporteerd naar Nederland. Deze veranderingen zullen naar verwachting een behoorlijke impact hebben op het land in het algemeen, en het dagelijks leven van de mensen in het bijzonder. Zo zal de hoeveelheid voedsel en de soorten producten die in supermarkten verkrijgbaar zijn geleidelijk worden teruggebracht, vooruitlopend op de komende maatregelen. Dit zal uiteindelijk persoonlijke voedselkeuzes en het budget beïnvloeden van iedereen in Nederland.\"", 
"\"Het is zeer waarschijnlijk dat in de nabije toekomst verandering zal plaatsvinden wat betreft een andere aspect van gender en seksuele diversiteit maatregelen in Nederland: genderuitingen die bepaalde LHBT+-mensen uitsluiten zullen aanzienlijk worden teruggebracht met de introductie van verschillende maatregelen tegen het onderscheid tussen vrouwen en mannen in officiële documentatie. Dit zal naar verwachting een behoorlijke impact hebben op het land in het algemeen, en het dagelijks leven van mensen in het bijzonder. Zo wordt informatie over gender al geleidelijk uit persoonlijke documenten verwijderd vooruitlopend op de komende maatregelen. Dit zal uiteindelijk de persoonlijke documenten van iedereen in Nederland beïnvloeden.\"",

data_check.title: Data Check
data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 44 files: 8 data, 1 code, 20 documentation, 7 materials, 8 output.
-  We found 8 tabular data files and extracted 948 columns from 5 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 5 study groups (ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, pilot1).
-  3 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd: if it doesnt stress us were not changing the system_correlation table chapter 3.xlsx: 73% of columns are free text, not variables; hnf8b: if it doesnt stress us were not changing the system_correlation table chapter 3.xlsx: 73% of columns are free text, not variables; the transformative side of societal stress_correlation table.xlsx: 73% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd: if it doesnt stress us were not changing the system_correlation table chapter 3.xlsx, hnf8b: if it doesnt stress us were not changing the system_correlation table chapter 3.xlsx, the transformative side of societal stress_correlation table.xlsx. We ran automated data-quality checks on 948 columns and found no issues. We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender, Race. 3 of 7 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machines and then completed a computer E-Prime task (Schneider et al., 2012).
Participants were given two minutes to verbally express whether they supported the constitutional model described and why.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd", 
    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `The Transformative Side of Societal Stress_Dataset Wide SPSS.sav` to `the transformative side of societal stress_dataset wide spss.sav` (in the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd); `The Transformative Side of Societal Stress_Dataset Long SPSS.sav` to `the transformative side of societal stress_dataset long spss.sav` (in the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

**2 file names in the code are not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd", 
    Outcome = "ran_ok", Detail = "", "Time (s)" = 167.3), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "the transformative side of societal stress_r analysis code.rmd", 
    "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = " "), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

22 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. #### SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

info.title: The Road to Liberation is Paved with Threats: A Biopsychosocial Perspective on Minoritized Individuals' Responses to Hierarchy-Disruptive Social Change

text.text: We thank Rodrigo Perillo Lopez for co-devising the manipulation of social change, co-revising the Genderism and Transphobia Scale, and helping with data collection of this study.
We additionally thank Victoria Perini for helping with data collection.
Struggles for the liberation of minoritized communities are rarely linear.

In the Netherlands, a series of proposals to change sex registration were brought forward between 2004 and 2019, yet some transgender people feared they could undermine hard-won recognition of their transitions and promote identity-blindness (Transgender Netwerk Nederland, n.d.).
text.formatted: In the Netherlands, a series of proposals to change sex registration were brought forward between 2004 and 2019, yet some transgender people feared they could undermine hard-won recognition of their transitions and promote identity-blindness <ref type="bibr">(Transgender Netwerk Nederland, n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: In Italy, the 2018-2021 DDL Zan aimed to criminalize anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination, but some within the community worried it would narrow queer liberation to punitive legal solutions, prioritizing punishment over prevention and leaving structural inequalities intact (Alliva, 2021).
text.formatted: In Italy, the 2018-2021 DDL Zan aimed to criminalize anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination, but some within the community worried it would narrow queer liberation to punitive legal solutions, prioritizing punishment over prevention and leaving structural inequalities intact <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alliva, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In Chile, the 2022 constitutional proposal promised unprecedented recognition of Indigenous and queer rights, yet it was rejected by 63% of voters amid right-wing disinformation, and among Mapuche and other Indigenous communities, enduring mistrust toward state institutions and the inclusiveness of the constitutional process (Duda, 2023; IWGIA, 2020).
text.formatted: In Chile, the 2022 constitutional proposal promised unprecedented recognition of Indigenous and queer rights, yet it was rejected by 63% of voters amid right-wing disinformation, and among Mapuche and other Indigenous communities, enduring mistrust toward state institutions and the inclusiveness of the constitutional process <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Duda, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">IWGIA, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In these cases, tensions emerged not from apathy or opposition but from concerns about strategy, identity, and justice, showing that social movements must contend with internal and external complexities: when change is finally at grasp, uncertainty and risks can shape its direction.

Studying how minoritized people navigate such crossroads is essential for understanding what it takes to sustain progress beyond the first breakthroughs, and against setbacks, uncertainties, and backlash.

Much of the social psychology literature on undermining factors in social change has focused on understanding and reducing negative reactions among dominant individuals (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018), or on what motivates minoritized people to engage in collective action in the first place (Simon & Klandermans, 2001; Watts & Hipolito-Delgado, 2015).
text.formatted: Much of the social psychology literature on undermining factors in social change has focused on understanding and reducing negative reactions among dominant individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018)</ref>, or on what motivates minoritized people to engage in collective action in the first place <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Simon & Klandermans, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Watts & Hipolito-Delgado, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, less attention has been given to the complex, sometimes conflicted experiences of minoritized people during social change, leaving their negative reactions overlooked or misunderstood, which are in turn, at times, wrongly used for victim-blaming.

Hence, in this study, we examined whether minoritized (LGBTQ+) individuals also experience negative reactions to change that stands to benefit them, by examining their adaptive (challenge) and maladaptive (threat) physiological stress responses to hierarchydisruptive social change, where with hierarchy-disruptive social change we mean material and systemic social change that aims to dismantle unjust hierarchies, and that is rooted in minoritized communities' objectives and social movements initiatives, compared to those of dominant individuals (i.e., cisgender-heterosexual, hereafter cishet).

According to the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996), when individuals engage in motivated performances, such as public speaking or collective action, they may experience challenge when they perceive sufficient resources to meet situational demands, or threat when perceived demands exceed available resources (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: According to the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996)</ref>, when individuals engage in motivated performances, such as public speaking or collective action, they may experience challenge when they perceive sufficient resources to meet situational demands, or threat when perceived demands exceed available resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We then analyzed how appraising the demands and resources of social change shapes such responses, via rated (Likert-scale) self-reports and expressed (coded verbal) responses, and explored their effects on critical action (i.e., expressed endorsement of change, policy preferences, donation behavior, and protest intentions).
Empirical social psychological research often treats social change as unambiguously beneficial for minoritized individuals.

Although social change is widely recognized as disruptive to institutions and cultural norms (De la Sablonnière, 2017), research has largely examined its psychological costs for dominant individuals, framing resistance to change in terms of ideological conservatism, system-justifying beliefs, social dominance orientation, and defensive responses to perceived threats to status, identity, and moral self-concept (Brandt & Reyna, 2012; Knowles et al., 2014; Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020). minoritized communities (Jost et al., 2012; Pérez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Although social change is widely recognized as disruptive to institutions and cultural norms (De la <ref type="bibr">Sablonnière, 2017)</ref>, research has largely examined its psychological costs for dominant individuals, framing resistance to change in terms of ideological conservatism, system-justifying beliefs, social dominance orientation, and defensive responses to perceived threats to status, identity, and moral self-concept <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Brandt & Reyna, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Knowles et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Scheepers & Knight, 2020)</ref>. minoritized communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Jost et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Pérez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, collective action research has shown that weak group identification, internalized stigma, or suppression of negative emotions can hinder minoritized individuals' support for social change (Radke, 2016).
text.formatted: Moreover, collective action research has shown that weak group identification, internalized stigma, or suppression of negative emotions can hinder minoritized individuals' support for social change <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Radke, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Among sexual minorities, internalized stigma can, for example, dampen collective action by weakening the motivational impact of perceived discrimination (Chan, 2022).
text.formatted: Among sexual minorities, internalized stigma can, for example, dampen collective action by weakening the motivational impact of perceived discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Chan, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While informative, these findings relied on cross-sectional designs or focused on attitudes toward the status quo, rather than responses to social change itself.

Their retrospective and self-reported nature may limit their ability to capture the more ambiguous and less consciously accessible tensions that minoritized individuals may experience as they actively engage with social change.

Consequently, we know relatively little about the underlying processes through which such tensions emerge, or how they might be navigated in ways that support both minoritized individuals' well-being and the pursuit of social progress.

To address this gap, the present study applied the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996) in an experimental setting to test whether minoritized individuals, compared with dominant group members, experience greater mandative (threat) stress, rather than adaptive (challenge) stress, in response to hierarchy-disruptive social change.
text.formatted: To address this gap, the present study applied the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996)</ref> in an experimental setting to test whether minoritized individuals, compared with dominant group members, experience greater mandative (threat) stress, rather than adaptive (challenge) stress, in response to hierarchy-disruptive social change.

text.text: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996) provides a psychophysiological framework for understanding how individuals respond to motivated performance situations, contexts in which people pursue goals under evaluation.
text.formatted: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996)</ref> provides a psychophysiological framework for understanding how individuals respond to motivated performance situations, contexts in which people pursue goals under evaluation.

text.text: Within this framework, threat has been linked to poorer performance, diminished well-being, and patterns of avoidance, defensiveness, or withdrawal, whereas challenge is associated with approach-oriented behavior, persistence, and more effective coping (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Within this framework, threat has been linked to poorer performance, diminished well-being, and patterns of avoidance, defensiveness, or withdrawal, whereas challenge is associated with approach-oriented behavior, persistence, and more effective coping <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These differences are particularly consequential in the context of social change, where sustained engagement despite setbacks, and commitment in the face of uncertain outcomes are critical.

According to the BPS-CT, task engagement is a necessary precondition for challengethreat responses to arise and is typically indexed by increased heart rate (HR) and decreased pre-ejection period (PEP).
Once engagement is established, challenge arises when individuals perceive their resources, such as knowledge, social support, or (collective) efficacy, as sufficient to meet situational demands.
Threat emerges when perceived demands, such as required effort, but also the danger, uncertainty, and risks present in the situation, outweigh available resources (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: Threat emerges when perceived demands, such as required effort, but also the danger, uncertainty, and risks present in the situation, outweigh available resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Challenge-threat responses are associated with distinct cardiovascular profiles.

Challenge is characterized by increased cardiac output (CO) and decreased total peripheral resistance (TPR), indicating efficient physiological mobilization, whereas threat is marked by relatively lower CO and higher TPR, reflecting vascular constriction and constrained responding (Blascovich et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Challenge is characterized by increased cardiac output (CO) and decreased total peripheral resistance (TPR), indicating efficient physiological mobilization, whereas threat is marked by relatively lower CO and higher TPR, reflecting vascular constriction and constrained responding <ref type="bibr">(Blascovich et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: These responses are commonly summarized using a challenge-threat index (TCI), which captures individuals' relative positioning along a continuum ranging from threat (lower scores) to challenge (higher scores; Blascovich et al., 2004).
text.formatted: These responses are commonly summarized using a challenge-threat index (TCI), which captures individuals' relative positioning along a continuum ranging from threat (lower scores) to challenge (higher scores; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Blascovich et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Research applying the BPS-CT to social hierarchies has shown a remarkably consistent pattern: When hierarchies are unstable or feel illegitimate, those low in status display physiological signs of challenge, such as low vascular resistance paired with high cardiac output, decreased cortisol, and heightened testosterone, reflecting an open and adaptive stress response.

In contrast, those high in status tend to show physiological threat, namely high vascular resistance paired with low or stable cardiac output, increased cortisol and testosterone, representing a more defensive and maladaptive stress response (Scheepers, 2017; Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020; Scheepers et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In contrast, those high in status tend to show physiological threat, namely high vascular resistance paired with low or stable cardiac output, increased cortisol and testosterone, representing a more defensive and maladaptive stress response <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Scheepers, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Scheepers & Knight, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Scheepers et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to emphasize that most research paradigms equated social change to relatively depoliticized gains or losses within the existing hierarchies, in other words, social mobility, rather than disruption of the hierarchies themselves (see Becker, 1967; Dixon et al., 2017b).
text.formatted: It is important to emphasize that most research paradigms equated social change to relatively depoliticized gains or losses within the existing hierarchies, in other words, social mobility, rather than disruption of the hierarchies themselves (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Becker, 1967;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dixon et al., 2017b)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, social change was typically operationalized as competition, interaction, or comparison within minimal group paradigms or tightly controlled intergroup encounters, with research on real social identities largely confined to interpersonal gender dynamics (e.g., Dover et al., 2016; Scheepers et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In practice, social change was typically operationalized as competition, interaction, or comparison within minimal group paradigms or tightly controlled intergroup encounters, with research on real social identities largely confined to interpersonal gender dynamics (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Dover et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Scheepers et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a critical question for BPS-CT research: How would minoritized and dominant individuals appraise and respond to social change that seeks to dismantle hierarchies rather than signaling opportunities for individual or ingroup upward mobility within the existing system?

Hence, our study conceptualized social change as hierarchy-disruptive, and, more precisely, structural, drawing inspiration from real-world social movements, centering the aspirations of minoritized groups, and aiming to disrupt existing hierarchies.

We modelled such social change after the attempted constitutional reforms that followed the 2019 Chilean uprisings, which sought, among other goals, to secure constitutional recognition and protections for the rights of trans people (Fernández, 2020).
text.formatted: We modelled such social change after the attempted constitutional reforms that followed the 2019 Chilean uprisings, which sought, among other goals, to secure constitutional recognition and protections for the rights of trans people <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Fernández, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, the motivated performance situation consisted of forming and expressing one's opinion about a proposed hierarchy-disruptive social change.
Such a speech paradigm is a well-established method for eliciting cardiovascular challenge and threat response.

We additionally considered this task a form of political action, as it was publicly oriented (participants knew their responses would be coded) and bore on collective outcomes (Arendt, 1958; Arsith, 2015; Russo & Amnå, 2016).
text.formatted: We additionally considered this task a form of political action, as it was publicly oriented (participants knew their responses would be coded) and bore on collective outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arendt, 1958;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arsith, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Russo & Amnå, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The task therefore required participants to actively engage with a prospective social change by considering its implications and articulating a position toward it, while maintaining experimental control over the conditions under which cardiovascular responses were elicited.
For minoritized individuals in particular, engaging with hierarchy-disruptive social change may involve distinct and potentially under-theorized demands.

Minoritized individuals are often subject to heightened moral scrutiny (Fernández et al., 2014) and may face pressures to conform to depoliticized and non-confrontational identities to gain acceptance (Duggan, 2002).
text.formatted: Minoritized individuals are often subject to heightened moral scrutiny <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Fernández et al., 2014)</ref> and may face pressures to conform to depoliticized and non-confrontational identities to gain acceptance <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Duggan, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, politicized identification can strengthen individuals' readiness to pursue collective goals and social change (Simon & Klandermans, 2001).
text.formatted: At the same time, politicized identification can strengthen individuals' readiness to pursue collective goals and social change <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Simon & Klandermans, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Expressing an opinion about change may therefore require minoritized individuals to critically consider the implications and responsibilities associated with transforming social arrangements affecting their communities, potentially intensifying the demands of the motivated performance.
Moreover, critically reflecting on social change may make structural inequalities and the implications of transforming them more salient.

Although such reflection can foster collective efficacy and mobilization among minoritized individuals (Chan & Mak, 2019), it may also carry psychological costs; for example, greater critical reflection on racism has been associated with more depressive symptoms among Asian-origin youth (Ni et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although such reflection can foster collective efficacy and mobilization among minoritized individuals <ref type="bibr">(Chan & Mak, 2019)</ref>, it may also carry psychological costs; for example, greater critical reflection on racism has been associated with more depressive symptoms among Asian-origin youth <ref type="bibr">(Ni et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although some resources, especially collective ones such as shared responsibility, solidarity, and efficacy, can buffer stress and are often salient in minoritized communities (Burson & Godfrey, 2020), their availability is uneven, fragile, and vulnerable to intragroup strain, particularly in the context of unprecedented or highly disruptive social change (de la Sablonnière, 2017).
text.formatted: Although some resources, especially collective ones such as shared responsibility, solidarity, and efficacy, can buffer stress and are often salient in minoritized communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Burson & Godfrey, 2020)</ref>, their availability is uneven, fragile, and vulnerable to intragroup strain, particularly in the context of unprecedented or highly disruptive social change (de la <ref type="bibr">Sablonnière, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: From a BPS-CT perspective, hierarchy-disruptive change may thus represent a context of chronically elevated demands in the face of unstable resources for minoritized people.
Ultimately, we expected minoritized participants to appraise social change as more demanding relative to their available resources, thereby eliciting a greater cardiovascular threat response.
We tested this expectation using both self-report and verbal measures to capture complementary aspects of participants' engagement with social change.
Because stress responses can unfold rapidly and involve less consciously accessible processes, retrospective self-reports may not fully capture the experience of the situation (Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Because stress responses can unfold rapidly and involve less consciously accessible processes, retrospective self-reports may not fully capture the experience of the situation <ref type="bibr">(Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, self-reported appraisals provide insight into participants' consciously perceived demands and resources, while verbal responses allow for a more open-ended examination of the political ambiguities, tensions, and competing considerations underlying these appraisals (Dixon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, self-reported appraisals provide insight into participants' consciously perceived demands and resources, while verbal responses allow for a more open-ended examination of the political ambiguities, tensions, and competing considerations underlying these appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Dixon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To further strengthen and contextualize our findings, we compared LGBTQ+ participants' responses with those of their more advantaged counterparts, cisgenderheterosexual participants.
Finally, we also explored whether responses to social change varied as a function of individual characteristics that may shape engagement with hierarchy-disruptive change.
Given potential heterogeneity in LGBTQ+ experiences, we examined participant gender as a possible moderator (Chan & Mak, 2021).
text.formatted: Given potential heterogeneity in LGBTQ+ experiences, we examined participant gender as a possible moderator <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Chan & Mak, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We also considered attitudes toward the relevant social issue, as prior research has linked more positive attitudes toward social change to greater challenge and less threat (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018 , 2019).
