text.text: Finally, political identification and solidarity were examined because stronger identification with, and solidarity toward, a minoritized group and their struggle may shape how individuals engage with and respond to social change (Chan et al., 2022; Saab et al., 2015; Subašić et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Finally, political identification and solidarity were examined because stronger identification with, and solidarity toward, a minoritized group and their struggle may shape how individuals engage with and respond to social change <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Chan et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Saab et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Subašić et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The present study investigated physiological stress responses of minoritized versus dominant individuals while expressing one's opinion about hierarchy-disruptive social change, focusing specifically on the constitutional recognition of trans and non-binary people.
We compared participants' responses to a social change condition versus a status quo condition.
We examined whether minoritized individuals would experience social change as threatening, even when they support it or stand to benefit from it.
We also sought to understand the underlying causes, focusing on demands and resource appraisals, and potential consequences of this tension, focusing on critical action.

We hypothesized that (1a) social change is more threatening than the status quo for both minoritized (i.e., LGBTQ+) and dominant (i.e., cishet) individuals; and that (1b) social change (vs. status quo) is more threatening for dominant than minoritized individuals.
In addition, we hypothesized that (2) higher perceived demands would be associated with higher threat responses, whereas higher perceived resources would be associated with lower threat responses.
Perceived demands and resources were assessed using both Likert scales (rated demands and resources) and thematic analyses of participants' verbal responses (expressed demands and resources).
In relation to these hypotheses, we additionally explored the possible moderation of gender, transphobic attitudes, identification, and political solidarity with LGBTQ+ causes.

Finally, we explored the effects of physiological responses on critical action, namely whether threat would be associated to endorsement of social change in participants' verbal responses (expressed endorsement), preference for hierarchy-disruptive (vs. hierarchyequalizing) policy change, donations to advocacy organizations, and protest intentions.
The preregistration included hypotheses, design, planned sample size, materials, and planned analyses (https://osf.io/pvqka/overview?view_only=04c7fd34eb1f490db695d2113360c84e).
text.formatted: The preregistration included hypotheses, design, planned sample size, materials, and planned analyses (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/pvqka/overview?view_only=04c7fd34eb1f490db695d2113360c84e">OSF Preregistration</ref>).

text.text: We conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007) for a mixed-model design with 2 within-subject x 2 between-subject conditions.
text.formatted: We conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.0.10 <ref type="bibr">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> for a mixed-model design with 2 within-subject x 2 between-subject conditions.

text.text: Assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), α = .05, desired power of .90, and a correlation of .50 between repeated measures, the required sample size to detect a within-subject main effect (Hypothesis 1a) was 68, and detecting a within x between-subject interaction (Hypothesis 1b) also required 68 participants.
Detecting additional moderation or mediation effects (Hypothesis 2) was estimated to require 130 participants.

Because data collection could not be extended beyond June 2024, the final sample consisted of 114 participants, providing sufficient power to test Hypotheses 1a and 1b, and approximately .80 power for Hypothesis 2.
We paid participants €10.00, or 2 ECTS, for their full participation.
The average age of the sample was 22 years old (SD = 3.07).
Fifty-seven (50%) participants identified as LGBTQ+, with 10 of them identifying specifically as non-binary or trans.
Sixty-six participants identified as women.
Most of the sample (96) was white.
Participants rated their subjective socioeconomic status using a 10-rung ladder scale, with an average rating of 6.98 (SD = 1.58).
Finally, participants' political orientation tended slightly toward the left, with an average score of 6.62 (SD = 1.68) on a scale ranging from 1 ('right') to 9 ('left').
We used a 2 (minoritized status: LGBTQ+; cishet) x 2 (state of change: status quo; social change) mixed design with repeated measures on the second factor.
In order to mimic the ecological progression of social changes, the order of state of change was not randomized.
Participants first completed a 10-minute online survey administered via Qualtrics (2023).
After giving their informed consent, participants reported how they identified in terms of gender (man, woman, non-binary/trans) and sexual orientation (heterosexual, LGBTQ+).
Afterwards, we measured political orientation, attitudes toward transgenders, ingroup and outgroup identification (based on minoritized status), and political solidarity toward LGBTQ+ struggles.
The online survey closed with demographic questions regarding age, ethnicity, personal and family income, and subjective socioeconomic status.
Between 24 and 48 hours after the survey, participants attended their scheduled laboratory session, which was conducted in the psychophysiology lab of the university.
Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machines and then completed a computer E-Prime task (Schneider et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machines and then completed a computer E-Prime task <ref type="bibr">(Schneider et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: During the task, participants first read about the status quo.
They verbally expressed their opinion about the text in two minutes, which was recorded via a microphone.
The task was followed by a manipulation check, and the challengethreat, demands-resources, verbal task appraisal scales, and the policy preference scale.
This procedure was then repeated a second time for the social change condition.
The lab session closed with two more critical action questions, and the debrief.
Complete materials and scoring procedures are available in OSF (https://osf.io/pvqka/overview?view_only=04c7fd34eb1f490db695d2113360c84e).
text.formatted: Complete materials and scoring procedures are available in OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/pvqka/overview?view_only=04c7fd34eb1f490db695d2113360c84e">OSF Repository</ref>).

text.text: Unless otherwise specified, questionnaire items were measured using 9-point Likert agreement scales (1 = not at all;9 = very much).
Participants read two texts describing the status quo and a social change concerning the constitutional recognition of gender identities.
Both texts were approximately 300 words in length and matched for style, readability, structure, and content.

The status quo described the 'constitutional gender binarism,' modeled after the exclusive recognition of male and female of the current Dutch legal framework (Rechtbank Den Haag, 2023), and described as impactful yet long-standing and stable (de la Sablonnière, 2017).
text.formatted: The status quo described the 'constitutional gender binarism,' modeled after the exclusive recognition of male and female of the current Dutch legal framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Rechtbank Den Haag, 2023)</ref>, and described as impactful yet long-standing and stable (de la Sablonnière, 2017).

text.text: The social change described the 'constitutional gender non-binarism,' and was inspired by Chile's 2019-2021 uprising and constitutional reform process which sought to include recognition of gender diversity, protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, recognition of diverse family forms, and commitments to improved sexual education (Fernández, 2020).
text.formatted: The social change described the 'constitutional gender non-binarism,' and was inspired by Chile's 2019-2021 uprising and constitutional reform process which sought to include recognition of gender diversity, protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, recognition of diverse family forms, and commitments to improved sexual education <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Fernández, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It was described as impactful, unstable, and unprecedented (de la Sablonnière, 2017).
Naming "transgender" and "non-binary" in the constitution remains unprecedented and would fundamentally disrupt gender binarism as an ideology and material condition, making it hierarchy-disruptive.

As such, the texts addressed a range of domains affected by gender recognition, including education, bathroom access, gender-affirming care, anti-discrimination, identification and name-change procedures, marriage and parenthood rights, employment, and legal jurisdiction.
Manipulation Check.

We evaluated the effectiveness of our manipulation of state of change by asking participants to rate both the status quo and social change on five dimensions: credibility, severity, novelty, instability, and uncertainty.
Cardiovascular engagement and challenge-threat responses were assessed using established physiological markers (Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Cardiovascular engagement and challenge-threat responses were assessed using established physiological markers <ref type="bibr">(Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Engagement was indexed by increased heart rate (HR) and decreased pre-ejection period (PEP), a measure of ventricular contractility.

Challenge responses were characterized by increased cardiac output (CO) and decreased total peripheral resistance (TPR), whereas threat responses were marked by unchanged or reduced CO and increased TPR.

Physiological data were continuously recorded using a Biopac MP150 system (Biopac Systems Inc., Goleta, CA), including impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG), and blood pressure (BP).

ICG was measured with a Biopac NICO100c module using four spot electrodes (two at the back of the neck and two on the back, 30 cm apart), delivering a 400 μA current and recording thoracic voltage to derive stroke volume (SV) and PEP (Sherwood et al., 1990).
text.formatted: ICG was measured with a Biopac NICO100c module using four spot electrodes (two at the back of the neck and two on the back, 30 cm apart), delivering a 400 μA current and recording thoracic voltage to derive stroke volume (SV) and PEP <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Sherwood et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: ECG (Lead I) and BP (NIBP100d finger cuff) were recorded simultaneously.
CO was computed as SV × HR, and TPR as [MAP/CO] × 80, with MAP obtained from BP recordings.
Data were recorded using AcqKnowledge software (BIOPAC Systems, Inc., 2023) and scored using the PhysioData Toolbox (Sjak-Shie, 2022).
Protocols are available at https://osf.io/k5gjq/.
text.formatted: Protocols are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/k5gjq/">https://osf.io/k5gjq/</ref>.

text.text: Measures were segmented into a 1-minute baseline and two 1-minute speech task periods.
Two independent experimenters manually scored and cleaned data, resolving discrepancies by consensus; data from five participants failed to record.
Following a reactivity approach, task-baseline difference scores were computed.
Outliers (>3.3 SD from the grand mean) were handled by excluding six implausible cases and Winsorizing three cases to 1% above or below the next highest non-extreme value.
text.formatted: Outliers (>3.3 SD from the grand mean) were handled by excluding six implausible cases and Winsorizing three cases to 1% above or below the next highest non-extreme value.

text.text: Finally, a unified challenge-threat index (TCI) combined standardized CO and reversed TPR scores, with higher values indicating greater challenge and lower values indicating greater threat.
Participants were given two minutes to verbally express whether they supported the constitutional model described and why.
The task was designed to elicit cardiovascular responses while also capturing participants' accounts of social change.
Rated Demands and Resources.
Participants rated how they appraised the constitutional gender binarism and non-binarism.
We measured demands (i.e., requiring effort, requiring knowledge and skills, and bringing uncertainties), and resources (i.e., having resources, having skills and knowledge, and receiving support).
Each item was rated from four perspectives (i.e., personal, LGBTQ+, cishet, the Netherlands).
For analytical purposes, the cishet and LGBTQ+ items were first recoded based on participants' minority status to create ingroup and outgroup items.
The 24 items formed eight subscales of demands and resources, with acceptable internal consistency overall (α = .60-.88), except for the status quo system demands subscale (α = .59).
Verbal responses related to social change were transcribed using AmberScript and subsequently coded manually.
Responses about the status quo were not analyzed.

Two coders analyzed participants' verbal responses using an adapted coding scheme from prior work (https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 3), grounded in the appraisal component of the BPS-CT (Blascovich & Mendes, 2000) and guided by reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2008).
text.formatted: Two coders analyzed participants' verbal responses using an adapted coding scheme from prior work (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd">Supplementary Materials Chapter 4,</ref> section 3), grounded in the appraisal component of the BPS-CT <ref type="bibr">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2000)</ref> and guided by reflexive thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Braun & Clarke, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The analysis identified perceived demands (e.g., obstacles, risks) and resources (e.g., assets, support) related to implementing a non-binary constitution.

We focused particularly on the multidimensionality of social change (i.e., the interplay of personal, collective, and systemic levels; see Pratto & Stewart, 2020), and on realistic vs. symbolic demands and resources (Riek et al., 2006).
text.formatted: We focused particularly on the multidimensionality of social change (i.e., the interplay of personal, collective, and systemic levels; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Pratto & Stewart, 2020)</ref>, and on realistic vs. symbolic demands and resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Riek et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The final framework comprised five demand categories and five resource categories (Table 1).
text.formatted: The final framework comprised five demand categories and five resource categories (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The first coder identified and counted category instances per speech, and the second coder reviewed the coding.
Interrater reliability was high (ICC = .88-.97, all ps < .001; ten Hove et al., 2024), with remaining disagreements resolved through discussion.
text.formatted: Interrater reliability was high (ICC = .88-.97, all ps < .001; ten Hove et al., 2024), with remaining disagreements resolved through discussion.

text.text: Table 1 Thematic Structure of Expressed Demands and Resources (Counts in Parenthesis)
Realistic demands (179)
The participant expressed concerns that the nonbinary constitution would be difficult or costly to implement or even fail to achieve the desired effects or to be implemented at all.
"I think that like changing it to like man, woman and non-binary still doesn't change the fact that our society is extremely gendered in kind of a binary way."

The participant expressed concerns related to cognitive and moral uncertainties, including confusion, worries about discrimination, and the emotional burden of understanding the challenges faced by LGBTQ+ individuals.
Um, I kind of find it quite hard to imagine."
The participant expressed concerns over the reaction of other people to the implementation the nonbinary constitution, fearing they may not support it or even attempt to stop it.
"I would imagine that it would get a lot of backlash from people who don't understand, and it would probably spark a lot of useless debates.
Um, so I'd be scared of that."

The participant expressed concerns about losing the certainties and privileges associated with living in a binary gender system, including comfort in navigating social spaces and the perceived loss of control over bodies and identities.
"So there should be a certain limit which will be difficult to.
Probably demarcate where the where people are given the freedom to.
Be who they are"
The participant expressed tension between endorsing (vague) progressive ideals and managing the practical consequences of the non-binary constitution.
"Trans non-binary people.
Deserve to be acknowledged, but I think it would have to be in a milder manner than was listed here, because it would just be too extreme."
The participant expressed that the non-binary constitution could bring tangible benefits, improving (LGBTQ+) people's lives, material conditions, and well-being.
"I just want things to be more simpler for queer folk.
I and this seems also to make it more freer for everyone."

The participant expressed that the non-binary constitution represents a moral obligation and a hopeful vision for the future, with some reasoning strategically in order to overcome the demands of change, especially uncertainties.
"It would require a lot of effort, but I think that would be worth it.
So people can be themselves and be comfortable in society being themselves."
The participant expressed that there is materially support by a community of people around them (often the LGBTQ+ community) or by larger institutions.
"…but a lot of people will feel really supportive, so I don't see why we wouldn't do it."
The participant expressed there is morally support by a community of people around them (often the LGBTQ+ community) or by larger institutions.
Moral appeals to shared values and responsibilities were prominent.
Rationalizations as resource (130)

Participants expressed rationalizations to justify their opposition to change, including minimizing the issue and typical transphobic arguments about faking identities, changing sex arbitrarily, opposing body autonomy, and concerns about a 'gender agenda' affecting children.
"I don't think so that we have to be completely gender neutral since still, I do, uh, recognize that the majority of people in the world are, uh, fall under the binary umbrella."

First, using a scale from 1 ("Very against") to 7 ("Very in favor"), we coded the extent to which participants verbally endorsed the constitutional gender non-binarism in the social change condition verbal task (expressed endorsement).

Second, after each condition of state of change, participants rated on a scale from 1 to 10 whether they preferred a hierarchy-equalizing policy (financial benefits for LGBTQ+ people) versus a hierarchy-disruptive policy (the nonbinary constitution) (policy preferences; see Klebl & Jetten, 2024).
text.formatted: Second, after each condition of state of change, participants rated on a scale from 1 to 10 whether they preferred a hierarchy-equalizing policy (financial benefits for LGBTQ+ people) versus a hierarchy-disruptive policy (the nonbinary constitution) (policy preferences; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Klebl & Jetten, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: At the end of the study, participants indicated whether they wished to donate part of their endowment to an LGBTQ+ cause, on a scale from 1 ('€0.00/0 ECTS') to 10 ('€10/2 ECTS') (donation behavior).
Finally, participants indicated their intention to participate in an upcoming protest on a scale from 1 ('not at all likely') to 10 ('extremely likely') (protest intentions).
Rated Appraisals of Verbal Task.
We included rated appraisals of the verbal opinion expression task to distinguish change-related effects from general speaking stress.

Participants rated challenge-threat (two single items per condition, indexed by subtracting challenge from threat scores), demands (demands, effort, uncertainty; α = .77 status quo, .81 social change), and resources (resources, knowledge and skills, support; α = .79 status quo, .77 social change) when expressing their opinion.
We included transphobic attitudes to control for their effects on cardiovascular responses.
We used 20 items adapted (https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 1) from the Genderism and Transphobia Scale (GTS) (Hill & Willoughby, 2005) (α = .93).
text.formatted: We used 20 items adapted (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd">Supplementary Materials Chapter 4,</ref> section 1) from the Genderism and Transphobia Scale (GTS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Hill & Willoughby, 2005)</ref> (α = .93).

text.text: Identification and Political Solidarity.
We included identification and political solidarity to control for their effects on cardiovascular responses.
We measured identification (i.e., solidarity, satisfaction, and centrality) with 14 items from Leach et al. (2008), focusing on solidarity, satisfaction, and centrality (α = .88).
text.formatted: We measured identification (i.e., solidarity, satisfaction, and centrality) with 14 items from <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Leach et al. (2008)</ref>, focusing on solidarity, satisfaction, and centrality (α = .88).

text.text: We measured political solidarity with nine items adapted from Neufeld et al. (2019): three assessing outgroup solidarity and six assessing commitment to LGBTQ+ (i.e., connection, responsibility, and confronting inequalities) (α = .79).
text.formatted: We measured political solidarity with nine items adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Neufeld et al. (2019)</ref>: three assessing outgroup solidarity and six assessing commitment to LGBTQ+ (i.e., connection, responsibility, and confronting inequalities) (α = .79).

text.text: To test Hypothesis 1a and 1b, we fitted three two-level multilevel models (MLMs) to examine the main effects of state of change and its interaction with minoritized status on physiological challenge-threat (CO, TPR, TCI), while accounting for repeated measures within participants.
To test Hypothesis 2, we fitted three additional MLMs testing the effects of personal and ingroup, and system rated demands and resources on TCI.
Models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in R (lme4 package, version 1.1-37; Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in R (lme4 package, version 1.1-37; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: All models were specified by sequentially adding factors, namely rated challenge-threat of verbal task (Hypothesis 1a and 1b) or demands-resources of verbal task (Hypothesis 2), political orientation, transphobic attitudes, ingroup identification, outgroup solidarity, solidarity with LGBTQ+ cause, gender identity, ethnicity, and subjective socioeconomic status.
The final model retained only significant predictors, to avoid overspecification (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The final model retained only significant predictors, to avoid overspecification <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Analyses to assess the robustness of the hypotheses are reported in https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 5.
text.formatted: Analyses to assess the robustness of the hypotheses are reported in <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd">Supplementary   Materials Chapter 4,</ref> section 5.

text.text: To further test Hypothesis 2 and examine potential sources of challenge-threat, we conducted a hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward's method, squared Euclidean distance) based on participants' verbal responses to social change.

Standardized expressed demands and resources categories were used to determine the number of clusters via agglomeration coefficients and dendrogram inspection, and cluster membership was refined using k-means clustering.
Differences in TCI across clusters were then examined using multilevel models (MLMs).

Finally, we examined how state of change, minoritized status, TCI, and expressed demands and resources clusters influenced critical action, employing linear models, multilevel models (MLMs), and ANOVAs.

Paired-sample t-tests showed that, consistent with our manipulation of state of change, participants perceived the constitutional gender non-binarism (social change condition) as more unstable, t(111) = 1.65, p = .009, uncertain, t(113) = -5.44, p < .001, disruptive, t(113) = -16.53, p < .001, and novel, t(113) = -5.02, p < .001, compared to the status quo.
text.formatted: Paired-sample t-tests showed that, consistent with our manipulation of state of change, participants perceived the constitutional gender non-binarism (social change condition) as more unstable, t(111) = 1.65, p = .009, uncertain, t(113) = -5.44, p < .001, disruptive, t(113) = -16.53, p < .001, and novel, t(113) = -5.02, p < .001, compared to the status quo.

text.text: Interestingly, people found the social change more credible than the status quo, t(112) = -6.71, p < .001.
text.formatted: Interestingly, people found the social change more credible than the status quo, t(112) = -6.71, p < .001.

text.text: Paired sample t-test indicated that, compared to baseline levels, HR increased in both the status quo, t(102) = -18.87, p < .001, and social change, t(102) = -12.79, p < .001, conditions.
text.formatted: Paired sample t-test indicated that, compared to baseline levels, HR increased in both the status quo, t(102) = -18.87, p < .001, and social change, t(102) = -12.79, p < .001, conditions.

text.text: PEP decreased significantly in the status quo condition, t(102) = 4.96, p < .001, and marginally in the social change condition, t(102) = 1.82, p = .072, compared to the baseline (Table 2).

text.text: Our verbal task was thus able to establish sufficient engagement to elicit challengethreat responses.
Following these preliminary analyses, we tested our hypotheses using MLMs on CO and TPR reactivity, as well as the TCI.
In keeping with Hypothesis 1a, participants exhibited lower CO in the social change condition than in the status quo condition, β = -0.16, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.30, -0.03], p = .019.

The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was not significant, β = -0.11, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.06], p = .189, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, the effect of social change did not differ between cishet and LGBTQ+ participants.
Notably, trans participants exhibited significantly lower CO, β = -0.25, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.46, -0.05], p = .016.

Finally, the effect of minoritized status was moderated by GTS, β = -1.19, SE = 0.54, 95% CI [-2.27, -0.12], p = .030, such that LGBTQ+ participants higher in transphobia exhibited lower CO (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Finally, the effect of minoritized status was moderated by GTS, β = -1.19, SE = 0.54, 95% CI [-2.27, -0.12], p = .030, such that LGBTQ+ participants higher in transphobia exhibited lower CO (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Contrary to Hypothesis 1a, participants exhibited similar TPR across state of change conditions, β = 0.04, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.20], p = .662.

The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was significant, β = 0.21, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.41], p = .036, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited higher TPR in the social change condition compared to cishet participants (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was significant, β = 0.21, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.41], p = .036, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited higher TPR in the social change condition compared to cishet participants (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Notably, trans participants exhibited higher TPR, β = 0.34, SE = 0.09, 95% CI [0.16, 0.51], p < .001.
text.formatted: Notably, trans participants exhibited higher TPR, β = 0.34, SE = 0.09, 95% CI [0.16, 0.51], p < .001.

text.text: Finally, the effect of minoritized status was moderated by GTS, β = 1.22, SE = 0.48, 95% CI [0.27, 2.16], p = .012, such that LGBTQ+ participants higher in transphobia exhibited higher TPR.

The interaction between minoritized status and being a woman was also significant, β = 0.31, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 0.61], p = .044, indicating higher TPR among LGBTQ+ participants identifying as women.

The interaction between minoritized status and OPS was marginally significant, β = 0.41, SE = 0.22, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.84], p = .063, suggesting that TPR may be higher among LGBTQ+ participants with greater solidarity with cishet individuals.
Contrary to Hypothesis 1a, participants did not differ significantly in TCI between the social change and status quo conditions, β = -0.11, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.26, 0.04], p = .140.

The interaction between state of change and minoritized status was significant, β = -0.19, SE = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.37, -0.01], p = .037, indicating that, contrary to Hypothesis 1b, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited lower TCI in the social change condition compared to cishet participants (Figure 3).

text.text: Figure 4 Threat-Challenge Index Across Minoritized Status and Transphobia Levels Effect of Rated Demand and Resources on Challenge-Threat

Corroborating Hypothesis 2, and when controlling for the interactions between the covariates SSES, IDS, GTS, ethnicity and minoritized status, MLM results revealed a threeway interaction between personal demands, personal resources, and minoritized status, β = 1.23, SE = 0.57, 95% CI [0.11, 2.36], p = .032.
Among LGBTQ+ participants, higher personal demands combined with lower personal resources predicted lower TCI (higher threat), whereas this pattern was reversed for cishet participants (Figure 4).

text.text: To further examine the possible sources of physiological challenge-threat, we conducted a cluster analysis based on expressed demands (i.e., realistic implementation, symbolic implementation, retaliation, status loss, value-interest conflict) and resources (i.e., realistic personal, symbolic personal, realistic collective, symbolic collective, rationalizations) of social change.
First, we conducted a hierarchical clustering using Ward's method and squared Euclidean distance on standardized variables.
The examination of the agglomeration coefficients showed a gradual increase in cluster dissimilarity up to a height of approximately 9, followed by larger increments in successive merges.
To balance statistical considerations with meaningful interpretability, we selected a cut at height 9, resulting in five distinct clusters (Figure 6).

Regression analyses showed that LGBTQ+ participants expressed greater endorsement of the non-binary constitution than cishet participants, β = 0.47, SE = 0.20, 95% CI [0.06, 0.87], p = .024.

With GTS included, this effect became marginal, β = 0.39, SE = 0.23, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.85], p = .092, and higher transphobia predicted lower endorsement, β = -0.28, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [-0.54, 0.03], p = .028.

Regression analyses showed that LGBTQ+ participants donated more than cishet participants, β = 0.67, SE = 0.30, 95% CI [0.07, 1.27], p = .030, particularly at lower levels of outgroup solidarity, β = -0.83, SE = 0.30, 95% CI [-1.42, -0.24], p = .006.

Protest Intentions Across Speech Clusters

In this study, we examined cardiovascular challenge-threat responses to hierarchydisruptive social change, namely discussing a non-binary constitution in the Netherlands, among LGBTQ+ and cishet individuals, and how these responses, shaped by demands and resources, related to critical action.

Contrary to Hypothesis 1a, participants showed lower cardiac output (CO) but no differences in total peripheral resistance (TPR) or challenge-threat index (TCI) when discussing the non-binary constitution versus the status quo, suggesting no overall increase in threat.
As expected, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited threat (low CO, high TPR, low TCI), but contrary to Hypothesis 1b, they even showed greater threat than cishet participants.
Within
LGBTQ+ participants, threat was higher among women, trans participants, and those higher in transphobia, with the opposite pattern among cishet participants.
Supporting Hypothesis 2, only among LGBTQ+ participants, higher rated personal demands combined with lower rated personal resources predicted higher threat (lower TCI).
However, ingroup and system demands and resources did not influence TCI.
Additionally, five clusters of expressed demands and resources emerged, mapping onto physiological responses.

Supporting Hypothesis 2, threat reflected unresolved tensions: concerned moralists (mostly LGBTQ+) combined failure and retaliation demands with moral hope and collective resources, while ambivalent supporters (more often cishet) struggled to reconcile values with status losses demands.
Resource-oriented cluster, individualist (mostly cishet) and especially collective strivers (mostly LGBTQ+), showed higher challenge.
Notably, rationalizing opponents exhibited challenge despite opposing change.
LGBTQ+ participants expressed greater endorsement of the non-binary constitution, higher donations, and protest intentions.
Higher transphobia predicted lower endorsement, while stronger ingroup identification and lower outgroup solidarity amplified protest intentions among LGBTQ+ participants.
Surprisingly, higher challenge predicted lower support for hierarchy-disruptive policy, and LGBTQ+ participants with high transphobia showed higher preference than cishet participants.
Finally, resource-oriented clusters, especially collective, exhibited high endorsement and protest intentions, while ambivalent supporters were low on both.
Notably, concerned moralists combined threat with high endorsement and protest intentions.

Research on intergroup challenge-threat, informed by the biopsychosocial model, has largely established that when social change is defined as upward mobility, low-status individuals view it as an opportunity to improve their status, and therefore exhibit challenge responses, whereas high-status group members view it as jeopardizing such status, and thus exhibit threat responses (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020).
text.formatted: Research on intergroup challenge-threat, informed by the biopsychosocial model, has largely established that when social change is defined as upward mobility, low-status individuals view it as an opportunity to improve their status, and therefore exhibit challenge responses, whereas high-status group members view it as jeopardizing such status, and thus exhibit threat responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Scheepers & Knight, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings complicate this conventional framing: Hierarchy-disruptive social change elicits threat among minoritized individuals and challenge among dominant individuals.

Accounting for these discrepancies, and in line with previous work, our cluster analyses showed that LGBTQ+ participants view social change as offering material improvements, while cishet participants focused on status losses.
Yet, we uncovered additional tendencies:

LGBTQ+ participants expressed more moral obligations toward progress and concerns about failure or retaliation, whereas cishet participants tended to struggle with conflicts between values and losses, rationalize their opposition to change, or recognize change as beneficial.
Thus, even when social change is intended to benefit minoritized individuals, engaging with it may be psychologically demanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate cardiovascular threat in response to social change itself among minoritized people, extending research on critical consciousness and Freire's (1968) notion of the "fear of freedom" by highlighting the physiological stress that may accompany liberation.

This highlights that social change cannot be reduced to uniform, symmetrical, and abstract opposition between majority/minority, supporter/opponent, or gain/loss (see Huddy, 2017; Subašić et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This highlights that social change cannot be reduced to uniform, symmetrical, and abstract opposition between majority/minority, supporter/opponent, or gain/loss (see <ref type="bibr">Huddy, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Subašić et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than reflecting singular linear appraisals, responses emerge from co-occurring tensions between demands and resources.

These tensions are embedded within enduring systems of colonial, heteropatriarchal, and capitalist powers, which structure differential stakes, risks, and opportunities for minoritized and dominant individuals (Goudarzi & García Ferrés, 2025; Becker, 1967).
text.formatted: These tensions are embedded within enduring systems of colonial, heteropatriarchal, and capitalist powers, which structure differential stakes, risks, and opportunities for minoritized and dominant individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Goudarzi & García Ferrés, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Becker, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: These are furthermore shaped by an interplay between individual and collective demands and resources (see Pratto & Stewart, 2020).
text.formatted: These are furthermore shaped by an interplay between individual and collective demands and resources (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Pratto & Stewart, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, rated demands and resources predicted TCI only within a three-way interaction with minoritized status, such that effects aligned with BPS-CT predictions among LGBTQ+ participants, for whom higher demands and lower resources led to higher threat, but were reversed among cishet participants, for whom higher demands and lower resources led to greater challenge.
Thus, our findings extend BPS-CT by empirically testing its central demandresource proposition physiologically and showing that this relationship varies by social position:
LGBTQ+ participants followed BPS-CT predictions, whereas cishet participants showed the opposite pattern.
One possibility is that, among cishet participants, higher demands and lower resources strengthened rationalizing opposition to social change.
These findings also invite reconsideration of the dominant focus on social mobility in intergroup challenge-threat research.

Although examining how minoritized and dominant individuals respond to social mobility is valuable, for example for predicting sexism or support for affirmative action (Scheepers et al., 2009), this perspective is not neutral.
text.formatted: Although examining how minoritized and dominant individuals respond to social mobility is valuable, for example for predicting sexism or support for affirmative action <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Scheepers et al., 2009)</ref>, this perspective is not neutral.

text.text: It inadvertently resonates with a neoliberal meritocratic logic in which equal opportunities within the status quo are treated as the primary marker of progress (Adams et al., 2019; Goudarzi & García Ferrés, 2025; Littler, 2018), despite ample evidence that improved social mobility does little to address structural inequalities (Littler, 2013; Sandel, 2020).
text.formatted: It inadvertently resonates with a neoliberal meritocratic logic in which equal opportunities within the status quo are treated as the primary marker of progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Goudarzi & García Ferrés, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Littler, 2018)</ref>, despite ample evidence that improved social mobility does little to address structural inequalities <ref type="bibr">(Littler, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Sandel, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This resonates with an emerging psychological perspective on collective liberation, which challenges progress understood as individual advancement and instead emphasizes interconnected struggles, solidarity, and collective transformation (Schreiber et al., 2026; Vestergren et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This resonates with an emerging psychological perspective on collective liberation, which challenges progress understood as individual advancement and instead emphasizes interconnected struggles, solidarity, and collective transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Schreiber et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Vestergren et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, this research has fostered a preoccupation with threat avoidance among dominant individuals as a means to achieve harmonious intergroup relations, which is often viewed as a primary pathway to equal opportunities (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018).
text.formatted: Moreover, this research has fostered a preoccupation with threat avoidance among dominant individuals as a means to achieve harmonious intergroup relations, which is often viewed as a primary pathway to equal opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Systematically centering dominant groups reflects a hegemonic tendency to produce knowledge from the vantage point of the majority and present it as universal (Reddy & Amer, 2022; Oswald & Adams Jr., 2022).
text.formatted: Systematically centering dominant groups reflects a hegemonic tendency to produce knowledge from the vantage point of the majority and present it as universal <ref type="bibr">(Reddy & Amer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Oswald & Adams Jr., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Generalizing from this perspective risks reproducing the status quo that it aims to dismantle in two ways.
First, by obscuring the negative experiences of minoritized individuals, it can exacerbate rather than reduce systemic disparities.

Second, it may end up prioritizing social change that minimally disrupts dominant comfort, thus overlooking disruptive forms that more effectively advance minoritized individuals' well-being (Lorde, 1979).
text.formatted: Second, it may end up prioritizing social change that minimally disrupts dominant comfort, thus overlooking disruptive forms that more effectively advance minoritized individuals' well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Lorde, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly consequential considering that minoritized people are both more directly affected by social change and more actively involved in its realization (Tilly & Wood, 2015).
text.formatted: This is particularly consequential considering that minoritized people are both more directly affected by social change and more actively involved in its realization <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Tilly & Wood, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Resonating with "fear of freedom," our finding suggest that while liberation is empowering, eliciting moral hope and collective efforts, it is simultaneously accompanied by heightened exposure to demands such as risks, uncertainties, and vulnerabilities for minoritized communities (Chan, 2024; Desmarais & Christophe, 2024; Freire, 1968; Maker-Castro et al., 2022; Martín-Baró, 1994).
text.formatted: Resonating with "fear of freedom," our finding suggest that while liberation is empowering, eliciting moral hope and collective efforts, it is simultaneously accompanied by heightened exposure to demands such as risks, uncertainties, and vulnerabilities for minoritized communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Chan, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Desmarais & Christophe, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Freire, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Maker-Castro et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Martín-Baró, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This may also account for higher threat in LGBTQ+ participants with greater transphobia, highlighting a tension between internalized oppression and critical consciousness.
Extending previous research, our results highlight that such tensions arise not only when minoritized people confront ongoing oppression, but also when they envision plausible liberation.
This has important implications.
Threat responses are considered maladaptive and have been linked to poorer well-being and health outcomes (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: Threat responses are considered maladaptive and have been linked to poorer well-being and health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: LGBTQ+ individuals are already disproportionately affected by (mental) health disparities, including elevated rates of anxiety, depression, and asthma, largely due to chronic exposure to stigma and minority stress (Hatzenbuehler, 2009; Meyer, 1995; 2003).
text.formatted: LGBTQ+ individuals are already disproportionately affected by (mental) health disparities, including elevated rates of anxiety, depression, and asthma, largely due to chronic exposure to stigma and minority stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Hatzenbuehler, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Meyer, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">2003)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly concerning, as threat was higher among LGBTQ+ women and trans participants, who face compounded forms of discrimination and health challenges.
Furthermore, threat is associated with freezing, withdrawal, and avoidance tendencies (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: Furthermore, threat is associated with freezing, withdrawal, and avoidance tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this account and with BPS-CT predictions, we observed that participants characterized by the highest levels of threat, such as the fewer LGBTQ+ individuals within the ambivalent supporter cluster, reported lower protest intentions and lower expressed endorsement of social change.
However, challengethreat was not reliably and directly associated with critical action.

The most striking pattern emerged among the concerned moralists, who combined moral commitment and collective resources with worries that social change might fail or provoke retaliation, while also reporting higher protest intentions and stronger endorsement of change.

Relatedly, LGBTQ+ participants expressed higher endorsement and greater protest intentions overall, particularly when they identified strongly with their ingroup and weakly with cishet outgroups, and threat (lower TCI) predicted preference for hierarchy-disruptive (vs.
hierarchy-equalizing) policy.

These patterns suggest that minoritized people may pursue critical action despite demands and threat, potentially at the expense of their well-being, especially because they have stronger politicized identification and feel more morally obliged toward change (Drury & Reicher, 2009; Klandermans, 1984).
text.formatted: These patterns suggest that minoritized people may pursue critical action despite demands and threat, potentially at the expense of their well-being, especially because they have stronger politicized identification and feel more morally obliged toward change <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Drury & Reicher, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Klandermans, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this extends collective action research, which has primarily examined factors that facilitate or hinder action, by highlighting that action may also persist alongside unresolved psychological tensions.

In this sense, our findings complement research emphasizing the risks and costs associated with collective action (Uysal et al., 2022) by suggesting that such risks may be accompanied by physiological stress responses.
text.formatted: In this sense, our findings complement research emphasizing the risks and costs associated with collective action <ref type="bibr">(Uysal et al., 2022)</ref> by suggesting that such risks may be accompanied by physiological stress responses.

text.text: Alarmingly, this dynamic resonates with research showing elevated burnout among queer activists and activists of color (Gauditz, 2024; Vaccaro & Mena, 2011).
text.formatted: Alarmingly, this dynamic resonates with research showing elevated burnout among queer activists and activists of color <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Gauditz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Vaccaro & Mena, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These findings reinforce the concern that, although hierarchy-disruptive social change is emancipatory, it may be detrimental to minoritized people's health and well-being.

By linking these tensions to cardiovascular responses, our findings furthermore offer a novel stress-and-coping perspective on critical consciousness and action, which allows us to investigate the sources of threat, but also possible coping mechanisms to address them (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: By linking these tensions to cardiovascular responses, our findings furthermore offer a novel stress-and-coping perspective on critical consciousness and action, which allows us to investigate the sources of threat, but also possible coping mechanisms to address them <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that threat and critical action may be dynamically intertwined rather than always strictly oppositional, and shaped by tensions between demands and resources, as shown by both rated and expressed measures.
Accordingly, threat may not be something to avoid or overcome, but a meaningful response that signals the tensions involved in engaging with more systemic and disruptive forms of social change.

Rather than suppressing or circumventing these tensions, approach-based coping may help individuals attend to and work through them, potentially supporting well-being and sustaining collective efforts under high-demand conditions (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: Rather than suppressing or circumventing these tensions, approach-based coping may help individuals attend to and work through them, potentially supporting well-being and sustaining collective efforts under high-demand conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Reliance on moral obligation, hope, and symbolic and practical collective resources, such as solidarity and shared responsibility, as seen among collective strivers and concerned moralists, may therefore help individuals navigate threat while sustaining critical action.

Previous empirical evidence highlighted that utopian thinking, defined as imagining better societies, increases hope toward progress, which in turn increases sustained commitment toward system-challenging collective action, among both advantage and disadvantaged groups (Badaan et al., 2022; Badaan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous empirical evidence highlighted that utopian thinking, defined as imagining better societies, increases hope toward progress, which in turn increases sustained commitment toward system-challenging collective action, among both advantage and disadvantaged groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Badaan et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Badaan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, moral obligation predicts collective action even under high-risk conditions (Uysal et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, moral obligation predicts collective action even under high-risk conditions <ref type="bibr">(Uysal et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Collective resource mobilization, such as organizational capacity and mobilizable resources, was found to be a main driver of Palestinian collective action in the West Bank, exerting stronger and more consistent effects than deprivation-based factors in opposition to Israeli illegal settlements and state repression in the past decades (Khawaja, 1994).
text.formatted: Collective resource mobilization, such as organizational capacity and mobilizable resources, was found to be a main driver of Palestinian collective action in the West Bank, exerting stronger and more consistent effects than deprivation-based factors in opposition to Israeli illegal settlements and state repression in the past decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Khawaja, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, collective resources are a well-established driver of movement building (Edwards, 2013), yet somewhat understudied in psychology.
text.formatted: More broadly, collective resources are a well-established driver of movement building <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Edwards, 2013)</ref>, yet somewhat understudied in psychology.

text.text: Extending this literature, our findings suggest that minoritized group members may be more likely than dominant groups to draw on moral hope and collective resources, and that combining collective with personal resources, rather than relying on personal resources alone, may offer a more effective strategy for coping with the demands and threats of social change.
These patterns point to promising avenues for future research and practical application.

For example, social movements could foster spaces where the demands and threats of social change are openly acknowledged and collectively addressed, rather than avoided or individualized, thereby supporting minoritized people's well-being as they navigate the demands and threat of hierarchy-disruptive social change.

As such, these findings provide initial empirical insight into the psychological processes of collective liberation, according to which liberation involves recognizing interlocked systems of oppression and taking shared responsibility for their collective transformation (Schreiber et al., 2026), while also raising the possibility that, alongside positive emotions, negative emotions may serve constructive functions in sustaining collective action (Vestergren et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As such, these findings provide initial empirical insight into the psychological processes of collective liberation, according to which liberation involves recognizing interlocked systems of oppression and taking shared responsibility for their collective transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Schreiber et al., 2026)</ref>, while also raising the possibility that, alongside positive emotions, negative emotions may serve constructive functions in sustaining collective action <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Vestergren et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To this end, insights from critical pedagogy may help movements collectively examine the individual and structural conditions producing tensions around social change and develop shared understandings of how to navigate them (Diemer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To this end, insights from critical pedagogy may help movements collectively examine the individual and structural conditions producing tensions around social change and develop shared understandings of how to navigate them <ref type="bibr">(Diemer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Work pedagogy of discomfort may help create spaces to stay with difficult emotions, question taken-for-granted assumptions, and engage rather than avoid discomfort (Zembylas, 2015).
text.formatted: Work pedagogy of discomfort may help create spaces to stay with difficult emotions, question taken-for-granted assumptions, and engage rather than avoid discomfort <ref type="bibr">(Zembylas, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging approaches such as tending grief may help movements collectively acknowledge and care for experiences of loss, while incorporating them into ongoing political organizing (Barton, 2024).
text.formatted: Emerging approaches such as tending grief may help movements collectively acknowledge and care for experiences of loss, while incorporating them into ongoing political organizing <ref type="bibr">(Barton, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present section, we reflect on the design and methodological choices that contributed to both the strengths and limitations of the study, as well as pointing and future research directions.
A first limitation is that the two states of change were not counterbalanced, leaving open the possibility of an order effect.
However, a generic habituation or fatigue account would be expected to produce more uniform reductions in physiological engagement and challengethreat responding (Hughes et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, a generic habituation or fatigue account would be expected to produce more uniform reductions in physiological engagement and challengethreat responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hughes et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, the second speech showed a shift from challenge to threat among LGBTQ+ participants, and to higher challenge among cishet participants alongside higher self-reported challenge and greater perceived demands and resources.
These cardiovascular effects also remained when controlling for task engagement.
Thus, although an order effect cannot be excluded, the pattern is more consistent with a response to social change than with simple habituation.
The fixed order was theoretically motivated by the status quo as a necessary reference point for evaluating change (de la Sablonnière, 2017).
Future work should nevertheless replicate these findings with counterbalanced designs.
Second, results regarding demands and resources reveal some inconsistencies.
Although rated personal demands and resources predicted TCI in line with our hypotheses and BPS-CT for LGBTQ+ participants, the pattern was inverted for cishet participants.
Additionally, although our cluster analyses highlighted the importance of collective resources, rated ingroup and system resources did not influence TCI.

We partly attribute these discrepancies to the inherent limitations of scale measures, which are less able to capture the tensions identified in the cluster analyses, such as resources emerging to cope with opposition, rather than support for social change.
Another possible explanation is that ingroup and system levels influence personal appraisal, which in turn shapes TCI.

Hence, we deem it promising to keep investigating demands and resources through verbal responses, with future research possibly relying on more in depth accounts, such as multiple questions, interviews, and focus groups.
Finally, the present study examined responses to a specific form of hierarchy-disruptive social change: the introduction of a non-binary constitution.
This focus was a key strength of our approach, providing a realistic, minority-centered operationalization of social change and revealing tensions often invisible in more abstract paradigms.

At the same time, using a laboratory-based speech task constrained our inferences, as findings primarily reflect responses to speaking about social change in a controlled setting rather than other forms of political action.
The study's focus on LGBTQ+ issues within a particular sociopolitical context may also limit generalizability, yet yield more ecological validity.
Notably, this study represents the first application of the BPS-CT to LGBTQ+ issues.
Future research could examine other social change topics, as well as find creative ways to test cardiovascular responses to other forms of political action.

Building on the present findings, future research could examine how threat responses can be actively navigated or transformed into challenge, and identify the conditions under which these processes foster both critical action and positive health outcomes.

In particular, longitudinal studies, whether in experimental lab settings or in the field, could track initial threat responses to social change and test the effects of collective interventions designed to manage these responses over time.

The use of participatory action research may be particularly well suited in combination with BPS-CT and the present insights, allowing researchers and participants to collaboratively explore processes that turn threat into a mobilizing force.
The present study shows that when social change is hierarchy-disruptive, it cannot be understood as a simple or symmetrical redistribution of gains and losses between groups.
Instead, social change involves historically and structurally situated tensions that are experienced differently across social positions.
For minoritized individuals in particular, liberation can simultaneously involve moral obligations and collective responsibility alongside physiological threat.
Importantly, these tensions do not necessarily prevent critical action; threat and action may coexist as people navigate the demands and resources involved in pursuing transformative change.
Our findings therefore suggest that threat should not be interpreted as resistance to social change or as an individual problem to be overcome.
It may instead reveal the psychological tensions involved in pursuing change; tensions that may need to be collectively acknowledged and addressed.

By bringing these tensions into the study of challenge-threat and collective action, our findings shift attention from how to make social change less threatening to dominant groups toward understanding what it demands of those who are most invested in, and most affected by, its transformation.
